content: A biophysical profile (BPP) is a diagnostic tool that involves ultrasound monitoring to evaluate fetal movements, fetal tone, and fetal breathing, as well as an ultrasound assessment of amniotic fluid volume. In some cases, it may also include an assessment of the fetal heart rate. The purpose of the BPP is to identify fetuses that may be at risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. If concerns are identified, additional evaluations of fetal well-being may be conducted, or interventions such as labor induction or cesarean delivery may be initiated to expedite birth. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of the BPP with conventional monitoring methods, such as cardiotocography (CTG) alone or the modified biophysical profile (MBPP), on pregnancy outcomes in high-risk pregnancies. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, was conducted. The search covered studies published up to January 2012, and the results were added to the awaiting classification section for further evaluation. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the use of the BPP with other forms of antepartum fetal assessment in women with high-risk pregnancies. Two independent authors assessed the eligibility and quality of the studies and extracted the relevant data. A total of five trials involving 2,974 women were included in the analysis. However, most of these trials were not of high methodological quality. The overall incidence of adverse outcomes was low, and the evidence from randomized controlled trials did not support the use of the BPP as a reliable test for assessing fetal well-being in high-risk pregnancies. There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of perinatal deaths (relative risk [RR] 1.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60 to 2.98) or Apgar scores of less than seven at five minutes (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.92). Data from two high-quality trials suggested an increased risk of cesarean delivery in the BPP group (RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.44, n = 280, interaction test P = 0.03). However, the number of participants in these trials was relatively small (n = 280), which limits the reliability of this finding. Additional evidence is needed to determine the efficacy of the BPP in high-risk pregnancies with greater certainty. Furthermore, the impact of the BPP on other outcomes, such as the need for additional interventions, the length of hospital stay, serious short-term and long-term neonatal morbidity, and parental satisfaction, requires further investigation. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence from randomized trials to support the routine use of the BPP as a test for fetal well-being in high-risk pregnancies. It is important to note that three citations in the awaiting classification section of the review may influence these conclusions once they are assessed.
